chunks: Motor and solenoid failure modes. The question: What are some failure modes of motors/solenoids? How can they be avoided?
Motors and solenoids are coils of copper wire that turn current into motion. They fail in four main ways.
They overheat, because current turns into heat when the motion is blocked. They make voltage spikes when switched off, because a coil resists sudden changes in current.
They wear mechanically, and they suffer from the environment. Each failure has a standard cure, such as current limiting, a flyback diode, or a duty-cycle limit.
Picture a water pipe with a heavy flow. Slam the tap shut and the moving water has nowhere to go, so pressure spikes and can burst a fitting.
That is the voltage spike from switching off a coil.
Now picture pushing hard against a wall: you spend lots of effort and nothing moves, so all of it becomes heat in your muscles. That is a stalled motor.
Most root causes fall into four buckets. Thermal and electrical stress are controlled by the drive; mechanical wear and environment by design and maintenance.
Stall: the shaft cannot turn. With no back-EMF, only the coil's (winding's) resistance limits the current. Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates against the supply.
Flyback diode: a diode across the coil that gives its current a safe path when the switch opens. Duty cycle: the fraction of time a solenoid is energized. It limits heating.
A 12 volts motor has a 2. 4 ohm winding. At stall it draws 12 over 2. 4 equals 5 amps and dissipates 5 squared times 2. 4 equals 60 watts.
That heat goes into about 30 g of copper, which warms by roughly 5 degrees Celsius per second.
From 25 degrees Celsius it reaches 155 degrees Celsius in about 25 seconds, which is the limit for common insulation.
Separately, switching off 1 amps in a 10 millihenries coil in 10 microseconds would give a 1 kilovolts spike with no diode or other clamp. That is the whole idea.
"Main failure modes are thermal, electrical and mechanical.
Stall or overload makes current V over R, and the winding overheats in seconds, so use current limiting, thermal protection and stall detection.
Switching off the coil produces an inductive spike that kills drivers, so use a flyback diode or snubber.
Brushes, bearings and plungers wear or stick, and solenoids burn out if held on beyond their duty cycle, so pull in at full voltage and hold with PWM. Derate and add fuses."
